Can CDW Corporation Restore Margin Momentum in the Second Half?
Fri, October 2, 2026 at 4:15 AM PDT 4 min read
CDW Corporation CDW has entered the second half of 2026 with a focus on improving operating leverage and expense efficiency after delivering solid second-quarter results. The company reported second-quarter net sales of $6.6 billion, up 10% year over year, while gross profit increased 6% to $1.3 billion. Non-GAAP operating income rose 7% to $556 million, and non-GAAP earnings per share increased 12% to $2.91. However, gross margin declined 70 basis points (bps) year over year to 20.1%, reflecting a greater contribution from large hardware infrastructure opportunities related to modernization and AI readiness, particularly among enterprise customers, along with a lower relative contribution from services.
On the last earnings call, management highlighted that the gross-margin pressure was primarily a function of business mix rather than like-for-like pricing pressure. CDW maintained pricing discipline and continued to pass through price increases, while the growing mix of infrastructure products, larger-dollar orders and enterprise customers carried relatively lower margins. At the same time, netted-down revenue streams increased 16.1% and accounted for 35.9% of gross profit, up 300 bps year over year. Services grew only 1% as customers prioritized hardware and cloud investments and deployment timing affected demand, although CDW expects life-cycle and professional services activity to increase as customers move from procurement toward implementation and management.
The second half is expected to bring greater benefits from CDW's Geared for Growth initiatives. Second-quarter non-GAAP SG&A represented 57.9% of gross profit, down 20 bps year over year and 410 bps sequentially. Management said the second-quarter improvement in operating leverage largely reflected expense discipline and broader efficiency measures, while the more significant benefits from Geared for Growth are expected to emerge in the back half. The company expects both operating leverage and its expense ratio to improve sequentially through the second half and into 2027.
For 2026, CDW expects gross profit to grow in the mid-single digits, although second-half gross margins are projected to remain below year-ago levels because of product and end-market mix. Third-quarter non-GAAP SG&A is expected to decline sequentially, helping reduce operating expenses as a percentage of gross profit both year over year and sequentially. Management also expects services demand to strengthen as current infrastructure projects progress into implementation, supporting its expectation for improving operating leverage during the second half.
ServiceNow, Inc.'s NOW margins remain under pressure as rising AI adoption and greater reliance on hyperscaler infrastructure increase costs. In the second quarter of 2026, non-GAAP total gross margin declined to 78% from 81% a year earlier, while subscription gross margin fell 250 bps to 80.5%. Despite the pressure, non-GAAP operating margin remained stable at 29.5%, supported by revenue outperformance and disciplined spending. For 2026, ServiceNow continues to target an 81% non-GAAP subscription gross margin and 31.5% operating margin. Management expects AI-driven efficiencies, including roughly $500 million in internal savings, to help offset infrastructure and integration-related margin pressures.
Accenture plc's ACN margins remained relatively stable in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, despite ongoing investments in AI, talent and acquisitions. Gross margin was 32.8%, slightly below 32.9% in the year-ago quarter, reflecting continued cost pressures from its labor-intensive delivery model and evolving AI-led services. However, operating income increased 6% year over year to $3.18 billion, while operating margin expanded 20 bps to 17% from 16.8%. SG&A expenses declined to 15.8% of revenues from 16%. Strong Managed Services growth and disciplined cost management supported profitability, although AI-driven delivery changes and higher acquisition spending could influence margins going forward.
Avnet, Inc.'s AVT margin profile is improving as higher volumes, favorable mix and operating leverage support profitability. Adjusted operating margin expanded to 3.8% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, up 73 bps sequentially and 129 bps year over year. Electronic Components margin reached 4.1%, while Farnell's margin rose to 9% from 4.3% a year earlier, supported by a higher mix of on-board components. Management expects Farnell to reach double-digit margins before the end of fiscal 2027 and consolidated SG&A as a percentage of gross profit to fall below 60%. However, gross margin remains sensitive to regional mix and pricing dynamics.

CDW Summit 2026: IT Leaders Seek a New North Star in the Age of AI | FedTech Magazine
IT leaders gather to share the latest technology insights at the 2026 CDW Summit.
New Research from CDW Explores AI and Cybersecurity
Learn how AI is helping IT teams manage risk and improve resilience.
IT leaders are the midst of an identity crisis. Long seen as back-office superheroes, some IT leaders now find themselves expected to serve as innovators, evangelists and even the “fun people.”
“I didn’t know that we were the fun people, man. Like, I was supposed to do one thing, now I have to worry about if it’s fun or not?” said Carollo Engineers CIO Andrew Ivey to his fellow panelist, St. Luke’s University Health Network Associate CISO Krista Arndt.
The two were having an introspective but casual discussion about how they were responding to all of the changes in the workplace and IT — especially those wrought by artificial intelligence.
But the setup for this conference conversation was different. The panel, which took place onstage during the 2026 CDW Summit in Dallas, had a podcast aesthetic to it and it was dubbed “CDW OTR (On the Record).” The two had big podcast mics in front of them, and Arndt was dressed more casually and sitting cross-legged on the couch. This could have been a conversation livestreaming from YouTube or Twitch.
Click the banner below to learn how organizations are unlocking artificial intelligence’s potential.
The idea that IT leaders would present themselves in such a down-to-earth manner would have seemed out of place more than five years ago. But this change in tone and style is a sign of the times. And the idea that it’s important to infuse fun, excitement or positivity into their IT management styles was one that Arndt clearly embraced more easily than Ivey, who viewed his role as an IT leader as more of an honest broker and a skeptic — especially when it comes to the AI hype cycle.
“I think it’s your responsibility to be the voice of reason and to help guide this. And if you don’t have a skeptic in the room, then guess what your job is: to be the skeptic,” said Ivey. “If you have a skeptic in the room, then it’s probably not helpful for you also to be a skeptic. But you need one. And so, go find one, bring them in the room, just so they can poke holes in this thing early on. And I think you’ll survive and build a bulletproof project if you just bring in a naysayer early.”
Arndt said she prioritizes a highly collaborative but honest and authentic approach to IT leadership. For her, having a positive relationship and effective communication with her non-IT counterparts is critical to her role as a security leader.
“Our technology organization has a phenomenal relationship with our hospital leadership, and they talk constantly,” said Arndt. “It’s something that we focus on a lot in security: speaking the language of people that we serve so they really understand what’s going on.”
Those conversations, which might seem more casual than they were in the past, are extremely valuable in Arndt’s pursuit of getting her non-IT counterparts to receive her concerns about risk management.
“Having those open conversations where you can just be yourself and feel like you’re not just trying to put on a show for your leadership … I do see that happening,” added Arndt. “They know there’s a lot of unknowns, but they’re really excited to investigate those reasonably and from a risk-balance basis.”
DISCOVER: How to optimize your agency's infrastructure for artificial intelligence.
Linking AI With Strategic Business Imperatives
As she walked out to the main stage to welcome the more than 600 attendees at the Sheraton Dallas Hotel, CDW Chief Commercial Officer Liz Connelly acknowledged that everyone in tech has been talking a lot about AI, and that many people are eager for the next step.
“OK, we know you’ve heard a lot about AI,” said Connelly. “We won’t be spending time simply admiring the opportunities and challenges around AI. We’ll be sharing our well-informed point of view on what to prioritize, what to build and what to do next. Because the question is no longer whether AI will change business. The question is how organizations can use AI to deliver real and measurable business ambition outcomes.”
To highlight just how CDW was putting its money where its mouth is, Connelly brought out the company’s recently hired chief strategy and transformation officer, Hang Tan.
Tan, who has been tasked with advancing CDW’s AI strategy, highlighted how CDW has decided to treat itself as “Customer Zero” as it deploys and learns from its own AI implementations.
CDW Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer Hang Tan speaks about CDW’s six AI imperatives, which are informed by its “Customer Zero” approach to AI, at the 2026 CDW Summit.
During his presentation, Tan shared six core AI imperatives that CDW has developed that he believes can also help guide its customers’ thinking around AI:
AI-ready infrastructure: “This is more than just securing GPU capacity, because when we're when we're talking about agents, agents will put entirely new demands across all of your infrastructure — your public cloud, your data center, your network, and your endpoints.”
Getting your data ready for AI: “This is all about giving AI secure access to your unique business context. But then, once you do that, your AI will start to generate data. How do you manage the AI-generated data, and how do you extract insights from that data?”
Activating AI in existing software platforms: “As these platforms introduce new agentic capabilities, you have a very tricky or important set of decisions to make: Where does it make sense to activate AI within each of your platforms, but where does it make sense to actually develop AI capabilities on top and across your platforms?”
Adopting assistants and agentic platforms. “Everybody here in the room are well down the path of adopting AI assistants, but the magic really happens when you move past the, ‘Hey, let's give everybody Copilot and have them experiment on their own,’ to how do you get to shared learning, shared experimentation, shared skills, shared agents? That’s where the benefit, the productivity, will really scale.”
Security: “How do you evolve your identity and your security controls to extend beyond just users, devices, but to also extend to agents?”
Financial discipline around AI: “It’s more than just tracking what the spend is or controlling the spend because, remember, if you really want to demonstrate business outcomes, you need to instrument both the AI, but also instrument your processes.”
The tone that CDW’s leadership was taking with AI was clear and focused on outcomes, and a sign that IT is intent on getting to a place of real progress when it comes to AI. The tech industry has spent a lot of time talking about how AI will change things, but many in IT are eager to see more proof of this change — and not just doomsday warnings or the frothy hype.
Humanoid Robotics Is Funny Stuff, but Also Serious Business
As Arndt and Ivey debated the state of IT and how drastically AI will reshape their industry, CDW Senior Vice President of Vertical Markets Mike Grisamore interrupted their conversation to bring out a special guest: CDW’s own humanoid robot, named CH3T.
The robot actually made its debut six months earlier, at the 2026 HIMSS Global Health Conference & Exhibition in Las Vegas. Nonetheless, the robot was an instant favorite with the audience at the Summit as it teetered out onto the stage wearing scrub pants and a Team USA hat, a nod to CDW’s role as an official sponsor of the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
CH3T comes out on stage to hang out with CDW’s panelists and moderators during the CDW OTR mainstage event at the 2026 CDW Summit.
“CH3T, by the way, those are some sweet scrubs you got,” teased Grisamore. “Apparently, when CH3T first joined us, CH3T came out, and having CH3T without pants on was a little disturbing to some of the nurses. So, CH3T now has scrubs, which are pretty sweet. And I know normally you wear your Crocs, like every good clinician does, but I do like the CDW red.”
While the bit between CH3T and the hosts was fun, and audience members seemed to marvel at the technical prowess of a robot that walked and responded to human interaction in real time, Grisamore noted that despite the lighthearted banter between him and the humanoid robot, CH3T was more than entertainment. He represented a meaningful investment on the part of CDW in promise of physical AI.
“We think about physical AI, and looking at them just as platforms, because we know that investing kind of in what’s next, it doesn’t always fit into everyone’s immediate budget,” said Grisamore. “Not that we have a massive budget to do it, but the opportunity to carve out a little bit and start thinking about, ‘All right, how do we take CH3T, or, you know, two generations past CH3T, and start thinking about, ‘All right, what are the use cases where there is a return on investment?’”
“We’ve got one of CH3T’s brothers that is pushing wheelchairs around, and we’re thinking about transport. We’re thinking about utilization, because CH3T, when he’s not pushing someone around in a wheelchair, he could be going and restocking supply closets,” added Grisamore.
Maybe CH3T is proof that IT can be about a little bit of fun and a little bit of business at the same time. And that IT is in a place where it can do more, be more and achieve more than it ever has in the past.

Q2 2026 earnings beat and Lovelytics deal
CDW’s current outlook builds on a solid earnings base from the most recent reported quarter. CDW's Buyback Pace Jumps: Can Stronger Cash Flow Sustain Returns?
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 5:59 AM PDT 3 min read
CDW Corporation CDW has stepped up capital returns in 2026, with share repurchases gaining notable momentum even as free cash flow (FCF) conversion remained below its historical framework during the first half. In the second quarter, the company returned $344 million to shareholders through buybacks and another $80 million through dividends.
First-half repurchases totaled approximately $545 million, already approaching the $653 million deployed during all of 2025 and exceeding the $500 million repurchased in each of 2023 and 2024. Including dividends, CDW returned $706 million to shareholders during the first half of 2026. The company also added $1 billion to its share repurchase authorization during the quarter, leaving more than $1.1 billion of remaining capacity and providing considerable flexibility for further buybacks.
The sustainability of this faster capital-return pace will partly depend on a recovery in cash generation. Adjusted free cash flow was $278 million in the first half, representing 42% of non-GAAP net income and falling below management's long-term rule of thumb of converting 80-90% of non-GAAP net income into cash.
On the last earnings call, management attributed the shortfall primarily to working-capital timing as CDW invested to support hardware-driven growth and customer demand amid elevated pricing. Inventory increased by roughly $400 million from year-end, but management expects to rationalize inventory as supply conditions become more normalized, making inventory reduction the biggest variable behind an anticipated improvement in second-half free cash flow.
CDW's balance sheet also provides some support for continued shareholder distributions. Net leverage ended the quarter at 2.5X, comfortably within management's 2X-3X target range, while liquidity was $2 billion. The company continues to target a dividend payout of roughly 25% of non-GAAP net income and remains active in evaluating acquisitions that broaden its capabilities and customer relevance.
Meanwhile, Geared for Growth initiatives are expected to improve expense efficiency and operating leverage during the second half and into 2027, potentially strengthening future investment and capital-deployment capacity.
ServiceNow NOW generated $2.257 billion of operating cash flow in the first half of 2026 and continues to target a 35% FCF margin for 2026. The company also expects around $500 million in internal AI efficiency savings this year, supporting cash generation while keeping headcount flat despite acquisitions. TTM cash flow conversion is 317.8%, above its 276.5% median, while FCF conversion is 274.3%, also above its 242.4% median. Strong cash conversion supports reinvestment and acquisition funding. However, the company's cash flow includes substantial stock-based compensation and acquisition spending, which should be monitored.
Accenture plc ACN continues to generate strong cash flow while returning capital to shareholders. In the fiscal third quarter of 2026, operating cash flow rose to $3.79 billion, while free cash flow increased to $3.60 billion. The company repurchased or redeemed 6 million shares for $1.2 billion and paid $1 billion in dividends, or $1.63 per share, reflecting a 10% increase. Accenture ended the quarter with $10.2 billion in cash, while $3.2 billion remained under its share repurchase authorization. For fiscal 2026, operating cash flow is expected at $11.5-$12.2 billion and FCF at $10.8-$11.5 billion.
CDW Price Performance, Valuation and Estimates
Shares of CDW have lost 5.9% in the past three months against the Computers - IT Services industry's growth of 6.4%.
CDW trades at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 11.27, below the industry's 17.23.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for CDW's earnings for 2026 has been revised marginally upward over the past 60 days.

Is the Options Market Predicting a Spike in CDW Stock?

Investors in CDW, Inc. CDW need to pay close attention to the stock based on moves in the options market lately. That is because the October 16, 2026 $175.00 Put had some of the highest implied volatility of all equity options today.
What is Implied Volatility?
Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. It could also mean there is an event coming up soon that may cause a big rally or a huge sell off. However, implied volatility is only one piece of the puzzle when putting together an options trading strategy.
What do the Analysts Think?
Clearly, options traders are pricing in a big move for CDW, but what is the fundamental picture for the company? Currently, CDW is a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) in the Computers - IT Services Industry that ranks in the Top 27% of our Zacks Industry Rank. The net effect has taken our Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current quarter to move from $2.91 per share to $2.92 per share in the same time period.
Given the way analysts feel about CDW right now, this huge implied volatility could mean there's a trade developing. Often times, options traders look for options with high levels of implied volatility to sell premium. This is a strategy many seasoned traders use because it captures decay. At expiration, the hope for these traders is that the underlying stock does not move as much as originally expected.

CDW Canada’s AI Workplace Trends Report Finds Canadian Organizations Entering New Phase of AI Maturity as Agentic AI Gains Ground
New research shows AI is moving beyond experimentation in Canadian workplaces, but trust, training and measurement remain critical barriers to realizing business outcomes.
ETOBICOKE, Ontario, September 22, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Today, CDW Canada, the strategic end-to-end technology partner that turns customer ambition into outcomes, released new research exploring how Canadian organizations are moving from artificial intelligence (AI) deployment to realizing business value. The report, Canada's AI Workplace Evolution from Adoption to Accountability, draws on a survey conducted by Earnscliffe on behalf of CDW Canada of 1,011 Canadian office workers across organizations of varying sizes and industries throughout Canada.
The report finds AI is now firmly embedded in Canadian workplaces, with daily use of workplace-approved AI tools nearly doubling year over year (31 percent, up from 18 percent). But as adoption becomes mainstream, organizations are increasingly focused on a more pressing challenge: turning AI investments into measurable business outcomes. The research also points to the rapid rise of agentic AI, with one third of employees already reporting the use of AI agents capable of completing multistep workflows, making recommendations and helping drive outcomes.
"AI adoption is no longer the story," said KJ Burke, Field CTO, Hybrid Infrastructure, CDW Canada. "Most organizations have moved beyond asking whether employees will use AI. The question now is whether those investments are creating meaningful business value. The organizations that lead in the years ahead will be the ones that can measure impact, build trust and reimagine how work gets done by empowering employees to work effectively with AI systems."
The next phase of workplace AI is already taking shape, signalling a shift from AI tools that assist with individual tasks to systems that can help execute more complex workflows and contribute to outcomes.
The research suggests organizations are beginning to move from simply consuming AI technologies to actively shaping them. Nearly one-in-three agentic AI users report their organization is already building AI agents in-house.
At the same time, the findings highlight the importance of employee enablement. Workers who receive hands-on AI training report significantly higher levels of confidence using AI (46 percent are very confident) than those who receive no formal support (23 percent), underscoring the growing need for practical, role-specific training as AI capabilities become more advanced.
"Agentic AI represents an important shift in how organizations think about AI," said KJ Burke, Field CTO, Hybrid Infrastructure, CDW Canada. "As AI evolves from assisting employees to helping execute work, organizations must invest not only in technology, but also in the skills, governance and trust required to use it responsibly and effectively."
Trust remains the biggest obstacle to deeper AI adoption
Employee attitudes toward AI continue to trend positively. Curiosity remains the dominant sentiment among workers (42 percent) and outweighs the percentage that are worried about AI, suggesting employees are increasingly open to AI in the workplace.
However, trust continues to be a barrier to broader and deeper adoption. Accuracy and reliability are among the top AI concerns across daily users (31 percent), less frequent users (24 percent) and those not yet using approved tools (43 percent).
The findings also show that barriers vary depending on an employee's experience with AI. More advanced users tend to focus on privacy and security concerns, while those who have yet to embrace AI are more likely to question both its reliability and its relevance to their role.
"The challenge for organizations is no longer generating interest in AI," said Ashley Otto, Senior Product Manager, CDW Canada. "It's helping employees trust the technology enough to use it confidently and effectively. That requires clear governance, practical use cases and ongoing education."
Organizations are beginning to see value, but many still struggle to measure it
The research suggests AI is delivering benefits beyond simple efficiency gains. Compared to 2025, employees with access to AI at work increasingly report improvements in productivity (58 percent, up 11 points), quality of outputs (54 percent, up 15 points) and innovation (48 percent, up 11 points), indicating that organizations are beginning to realize broader business value from AI investments.
Despite this progress, many organizations continue to face a measurement gap. While more organizations report tracking specific KPIs to evaluate AI performance than they did a year ago (38 percent, up from 24 percent), a significant number still lack formal frameworks to assess ROI (23 percent) or are unsure whether such measurement exists (23 percent).
As AI programs mature and investment scrutiny intensifies, the ability to measure and communicate impact is critical to ensuring effective adoption. For CDW Canada, that means helping organizations move beyond AI implementation to building sustainable programs grounded in strategy, employee enablement, governance and measurable business outcomes.
"Most organizations can tell you how many employees have access to AI," said Burke. "Far fewer can clearly demonstrate what AI has changed for their business. We're entering an accountability phase where success will be defined not by access or experimentation, but by an organization's ability to prove value and sustain results."
For Canadian organizations, the next phase of AI success will be defined by trust, workforce readiness and measurable outcomes. As organizations explore emerging technologies such as agentic AI, CDW Canada is helping customers build the strategies, skills and governance frameworks needed to turn AI investments into lasting business value.
To learn more about the state of AI in Canadian workplaces, download the full 2026 Canadian AI Workspace Trends Report: Canada's AI Workplace Evolution from Adoption to Accountability.
Join the conversation online by following @CDWCanada on X and LinkedIn.
This study was conducted by Earnscliffe on behalf of CDW Canada. Earnscliffe is a member of CRIC and abides by the ESOMAR code of Market, Opinion, and Social Research and Data Analytics and CRIC standards, including the CRIC Public Opinion Research Standards and Disclosure Requirements.
The online survey was in field from June 15 to 25, 2026, with a sample of 1,011 Canadian office workers who work in organizations with at least 20 employees and use a computer in an office setting 11 or more hours a week, using Leger's LEO panel. Amkor Technology Announces Phase 2 of Arizona Advanced Packaging and Test Campus; Expands Investment to $12 Billion
Strong customer commitments support 60,000 square meter expansion of U.S. advanced packaging capacity
TEMPE, Ariz.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sep. 8, 2026--
Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR), a leading provider of outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services, today announced phase 2 of its Arizona Advanced packaging and test campus. Driven by strong customer commitments that have surpassed the 33,000 square meters of cleanroom capacity planned for phase 1, the phase 2 expansion is expected to add 60,000 square meters and bring the campus to approximately 93,000 square meters of cleanroom space. The expansion increases the project’s planned investment to approximately $12 billion.
Designed from the outset as a multi-phase project, Amkor’s Arizona campus, which includes wafer bump, probe, assembly and test capabilities, is being developed to support long-term demand for advanced semiconductor packaging and test services in the U.S. Phase 2 expands manufacturing scale, and together with phase 1 is expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 Arizona-based employees.
“This next phase reflects the confidence our customers have placed in Amkor, the critical role advanced packaging plays in enabling the future of semiconductor innovation, and the strategic importance of our Arizona campus,” said Kevin Engel, president and chief executive officer of Amkor Technology. “As chip architectures become more complex, customers need a trusted partner that can deliver at scale with the quality, technology leadership and operational discipline required for their most advanced products, and it is critical to have that capacity in the U.S.”
Amkor’s Arizona campus is the first OSAT production site in the U.S. for advanced packaging in high volume, giving customers access to a full domestic turnkey manufacturing platform. Construction of phase 2 is anticipated to begin late 2027, with completion expected by the end of 2029. Amkor’s Arizona 170-acre campus allows for further expansion as needed to support customer demand.
About Amkor Technology, Inc.
Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR) is the world’s largest U.S. headquartered OSAT and is a global leader in outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services. With a strong track record of innovation, a broad and diverse geographic footprint and solid partnerships with lead customers, Amkor delivers high-quality solutions that enable the world’s leading semiconductor and electronics companies to bring advanced technologies to market. The company’s comprehensive portfolio includes advanced packaging, wafer-level processing, and system-in-package solutions targeting applications for smartphones, data centers, artificial intelligence, automobiles and wearables. For more information visit amkor.com.

Amkor vs. AXT: Which Semiconductor Stock Is the Better Buy Now?
Amkor Technology AMKR is a major outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider, offering advanced packaging solutions for AI, high-performance computing, automotive and communications markets. AXT, Inc. AXTI manufactures compound-semiconductor substrates, including indium phosphide and gallium arsenide, which are used in optical communications and other high-performance applications.
Although the companies serve different parts of the semiconductor supply chain, both are benefiting from rising investment in AI infrastructure. Amkor recently reported record second-quarter 2026 revenues and is expanding its advanced-packaging capacity, while AXT posted record quarterly indium phosphide revenues amid strong data-center optical demand. These developments make AMKR and AXTI an interesting comparison for investors seeking exposure to semiconductor and AI-infrastructure growth.
But which stock offers greater upside potential today? Let's compare the companies' recent performance, growth opportunities and key risks to see how AMKR and AXTI stack up.
Amkor offers exposure to the semiconductor supply chain through outsourced semiconductor packaging and test (OSAT), with advanced packaging becoming increasingly important as AI and high-performance computing (HPC) chips grow more complex. The company's second-quarter 2026 results showed this opportunity gaining traction: revenues reached a record $1.9 billion, up 26% year over year, while gross margin expanded to 16.8% from 12% and net income attributable to Amkor rose to $174 million from $54 million.
Growth prospects are increasingly tied to AI/HPC and advanced packaging. Amkor has active programs spanning 2.5D, high-density fan-out and co-packaged optics, while a new data-center CPU program began ramping in the second quarter and is expected to scale through the second half. Computing revenues rose 20% sequentially in the second quarter and were expected to increase nearly 30% sequentially in the third quarter, driven by AI data-center demand and the HDFO CPU ramp. Automotive & Industrial revenues advanced 17% sequentially, with ADAS the primary growth driver.
Strategic customer agreements strengthen the opportunity. A 10-year advanced-packaging agreement with TSMC is designed to expand U.S. packaging and test capacity, while a multi-year NVIDIA partnership targets next-generation AI infrastructure. Amkor expects a $1.5 billion NVIDIA-related customer prepayment in 2027, with services expected to extend roughly five to 10 years. Its Arizona facility is intended to provide high-volume advanced packaging and test capacity in the United States, while expansions in Korea, Vietnam, Portugal and Taiwan increase geographic flexibility.
However, investors should weigh these opportunities against Amkor's semiconductor cyclicality, heavy capital requirements, customer concentration, supply-chain and memory constraints, intense OSAT competition and dependence on sustained AI/HPC packaging demand. The company spent $688 million on capital expenditures in the first half and expects $2.5-$3 billion for 2026. Therefore, a slowdown in AI infrastructure investment could lead to excess capacity, lower utilization and pricing pressure.
AXT is benefiting from strong demand for compound-semiconductor substrates as AI data centers increase their use of high-speed optical connectivity. In the second quarter of 2026, revenues surged 164.8% year over year to $47.6 million, while GAAP gross margin expanded to 44.9% from 8% and GAAP net income reached $11.1 million, versus a $7 million loss a year earlier. Substrate revenues rose 232.7% to $37.6 million, driven primarily by InP demand for data centers and passive optical networks.
The strongest opportunity is indium phosphide (InP), which is emerging as the company's primary growth driver. Second-quarter InP revenues reached a record $30.7 million, while backlog exceeded $100 million. Management said customer demand continues to outpace supply and expects InP revenue opportunity to more than triple by year-end 2026. AXT is doubling InP capacity in 2026, plans another major expansion in 2027 and is progressing toward 6-inch InP substrates, which can support higher-value applications. Demand is being driven by 800G/1.6T transceivers and longer-term co-packaged optics.
AXT has recently deepened relationships with key optical-component customers supporting AI data-center connectivity. It has secured supply agreements with Casela and Coherent and a long-term capacity reservation agreement with Lumentum. These agreements provide greater revenue visibility, validate strong customer demand and support AXT's capacity expansion.
Despite AXT's strong growth prospects, its outlook remains exposed to several operational and geopolitical risks. The company manufactures its wafer substrates in China, making its business vulnerable to changing export controls, tariffs and trade restrictions. Notably, China's export-permit requirement for InP wafers remains a significant concern and can affect the timing of shipments and revenue recognition. AXT also faces semiconductor demand cyclicality, customer order volatility and the risk that major customers reduce, delay or cancel orders. In addition, maintaining high wafer yields and meeting stringent customer specifications are critical, as quality issues can lead to product returns, lower orders and higher manufacturing costs.
How Does the Zacks Consensus Estimate Compare for AMKR & AXTI?
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for AMKR's 2026 and 2027 revenues stands at $7.64 billion and $8.55 billion, respectively, giving Amkor a significantly larger revenue base than AXT. The consensus mark for AMKR's 2026 and 2027 earnings is pegged at $2.60 and $2.72 per share, implying growth of 73.3% and 4.3%, respectively. The earnings estimates have remained stable over the past seven days.
In comparison, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for AXTI's 2026 and 2027 revenues stands at $217.6 million and $453.6 million, respectively. The consensus mark for AXTI's 2026 and 2027 earnings is pegged at 86 cents and $2.20 per share, indicating 309.8% and 155.8% growth, respectively. AXTI's earnings estimates have also remained unchanged over the past seven days.
AMKR vs. AXTI: Price Performance & Valuation Check
AMKR has outpaced AXTI over the past month, with its shares gaining 9.8% compared with a 7.7% rise for AXTI, reflecting stronger recent momentum.
From a valuation perspective, AMKR appears more attractively valued than AXTI. Amkor carries a more favorable Zacks Value Score of B, compared with AXTI's value score of F. AMKR also trades at a forward 12-month price-to-sales ratio of 1.6X, significantly below AXTI's 12.26X.
Amkor and AXT are both positioned to benefit from growing AI infrastructure spending, with AMKR benefiting from advanced packaging demand and AXTI from strong InP substrate demand for optical connectivity. AMKR's growth is supported by expanding AI/HPC packaging programs, strategic partnerships and capacity expansion across key manufacturing locations. AXTI, meanwhile, has a strong InP growth opportunity, supported by record revenues, a growing backlog and capacity expansion plans, but remains more exposed to external factors, including geopolitical and customer-related risks.
However, Amkor's stronger revenue scale, more diversified business, favorable valuation and solid earnings outlook make it a better pick for investors than AXTI, though both stocks sport a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) at present.

Amkor Technology, Inc.
Amkor Technology Announces Phase 2 of Arizona Advanced Packaging and Test Campus; Expands Investment to $12 Billion
Strong customer commitments support 60,000 square meter expansion of U.S. advanced packaging capacity
TEMPE, Ariz.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sep. 8, 2026--
Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR), a leading provider of outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services, today announced phase 2 of its Arizona Advanced packaging and test campus. Driven by strong customer commitments that have surpassed the 33,000 square meters of cleanroom capacity planned for phase 1, the phase 2 expansion is expected to add 60,000 square meters and bring the campus to approximately 93,000 square meters of cleanroom space. The expansion increases the project’s planned investment to approximately $12 billion.
Designed from the outset as a multi-phase project, Amkor’s Arizona campus, which includes wafer bump, probe, assembly and test capabilities, is being developed to support long-term demand for advanced semiconductor packaging and test services in the U.S. Phase 2 expands manufacturing scale, and together with phase 1 is expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 Arizona-based employees.
“This next phase reflects the confidence our customers have placed in Amkor, the critical role advanced packaging plays in enabling the future of semiconductor innovation, and the strategic importance of our Arizona campus,” said Kevin Engel, president and chief executive officer of Amkor Technology. “As chip architectures become more complex, customers need a trusted partner that can deliver at scale with the quality, technology leadership and operational discipline required for their most advanced products, and it is critical to have that capacity in the U.S.”
Amkor’s Arizona campus is the first OSAT production site in the U.S. for advanced packaging in high volume, giving customers access to a full domestic turnkey manufacturing platform. Construction of phase 2 is anticipated to begin late 2027, with completion expected by the end of 2029. Amkor’s Arizona 170-acre campus allows for further expansion as needed to support customer demand.
About Amkor Technology, Inc.
Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR) is the world’s largest U.S. headquartered OSAT and is a global leader in outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services. With a strong track record of innovation, a broad and diverse geographic footprint and solid partnerships with lead customers, Amkor delivers high-quality solutions that enable the world’s leading semiconductor and electronics companies to bring advanced technologies to market. The company’s comprehensive portfolio includes advanced packaging, wafer-level processing, and system-in-package solutions targeting applications for smartphones, data centers, artificial intelligence, automobiles and wearables. For more information visit amkor.com.

Amkor vs. AXT: Which Semiconductor Stock Is the Better Buy Now?
Amkor Technology AMKR is a major outsourced semiconductor assembly and test provider, offering advanced packaging solutions for AI, high-performance computing, automotive and communications markets. AXT, Inc. AXTI manufactures compound-semiconductor substrates, including indium phosphide and gallium arsenide, which are used in optical communications and other high-performance applications.
Although the companies serve different parts of the semiconductor supply chain, both are benefiting from rising investment in AI infrastructure. Amkor recently reported record second-quarter 2026 revenues and is expanding its advanced-packaging capacity, while AXT posted record quarterly indium phosphide revenues amid strong data-center optical demand. These developments make AMKR and AXTI an interesting comparison for investors seeking exposure to semiconductor and AI-infrastructure growth.
But which stock offers greater upside potential today? Let's compare the companies' recent performance, growth opportunities and key risks to see how AMKR and AXTI stack up.
Amkor offers exposure to the semiconductor supply chain through outsourced semiconductor packaging and test (OSAT), with advanced packaging becoming increasingly important as AI and high-performance computing (HPC) chips grow more complex. The company's second-quarter 2026 results showed this opportunity gaining traction: revenues reached a record $1.9 billion, up 26% year over year, while gross margin expanded to 16.8% from 12% and net income attributable to Amkor rose to $174 million from $54 million.
Growth prospects are increasingly tied to AI/HPC and advanced packaging. Amkor has active programs spanning 2.5D, high-density fan-out and co-packaged optics, while a new data-center CPU program began ramping in the second quarter and is expected to scale through the second half. Computing revenues rose 20% sequentially in the second quarter and were expected to increase nearly 30% sequentially in the third quarter, driven by AI data-center demand and the HDFO CPU ramp. Automotive & Industrial revenues advanced 17% sequentially, with ADAS the primary growth driver.
Strategic customer agreements strengthen the opportunity. A 10-year advanced-packaging agreement with TSMC is designed to expand U.S. packaging and test capacity, while a multi-year NVIDIA partnership targets next-generation AI infrastructure. Amkor expects a $1.5 billion NVIDIA-related customer prepayment in 2027, with services expected to extend roughly five to 10 years. Its Arizona facility is intended to provide high-volume advanced packaging and test capacity in the United States, while expansions in Korea, Vietnam, Portugal and Taiwan increase geographic flexibility.
However, investors should weigh these opportunities against Amkor's semiconductor cyclicality, heavy capital requirements, customer concentration, supply-chain and memory constraints, intense OSAT competition and dependence on sustained AI/HPC packaging demand. The company spent $688 million on capital expenditures in the first half and expects $2.5-$3 billion for 2026. Therefore, a slowdown in AI infrastructure investment could lead to excess capacity, lower utilization and pricing pressure.
AXT is benefiting from strong demand for compound-semiconductor substrates as AI data centers increase their use of high-speed optical connectivity. In the second quarter of 2026, revenues surged 164.8% year over year to $47.6 million, while GAAP gross margin expanded to 44.9% from 8% and GAAP net income reached $11.1 million, versus a $7 million loss a year earlier. Substrate revenues rose 232.7% to $37.6 million, driven primarily by InP demand for data centers and passive optical networks.
The strongest opportunity is indium phosphide (InP), which is emerging as the company's primary growth driver. Second-quarter InP revenues reached a record $30.7 million, while backlog exceeded $100 million. Management said customer demand continues to outpace supply and expects InP revenue opportunity to more than triple by year-end 2026. AXT is doubling InP capacity in 2026, plans another major expansion in 2027 and is progressing toward 6-inch InP substrates, which can support higher-value applications. Demand is being driven by 800G/1.6T transceivers and longer-term co-packaged optics.
AXT has recently deepened relationships with key optical-component customers supporting AI data-center connectivity. It has secured supply agreements with Casela and Coherent and a long-term capacity reservation agreement with Lumentum. These agreements provide greater revenue visibility, validate strong customer demand and support AXT's capacity expansion.
Despite AXT's strong growth prospects, its outlook remains exposed to several operational and geopolitical risks. The company manufactures its wafer substrates in China, making its business vulnerable to changing export controls, tariffs and trade restrictions. Notably, China's export-permit requirement for InP wafers remains a significant concern and can affect the timing of shipments and revenue recognition. AXT also faces semiconductor demand cyclicality, customer order volatility and the risk that major customers reduce, delay or cancel orders. In addition, maintaining high wafer yields and meeting stringent customer specifications are critical, as quality issues can lead to product returns, lower orders and higher manufacturing costs.
How Does the Zacks Consensus Estimate Compare for AMKR & AXTI?
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for AMKR's 2026 and 2027 revenues stands at $7.64 billion and $8.55 billion, respectively, giving Amkor a significantly larger revenue base than AXT. The consensus mark for AMKR's 2026 and 2027 earnings is pegged at $2.60 and $2.72 per share, implying growth of 73.3% and 4.3%, respectively. The earnings estimates have remained stable over the past seven days.
In comparison, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for AXTI's 2026 and 2027 revenues stands at $217.6 million and $453.6 million, respectively. The consensus mark for AXTI's 2026 and 2027 earnings is pegged at 86 cents and $2.20 per share, indicating 309.8% and 155.8% growth, respectively. AXTI's earnings estimates have also remained unchanged over the past seven days.
AMKR vs. AXTI: Price Performance & Valuation Check
AMKR has outpaced AXTI over the past month, with its shares gaining 9.8% compared with a 7.7% rise for AXTI, reflecting stronger recent momentum.
From a valuation perspective, AMKR appears more attractively valued than AXTI. Amkor carries a more favorable Zacks Value Score of B, compared with AXTI's value score of F. AMKR also trades at a forward 12-month price-to-sales ratio of 1.6X, significantly below AXTI's 12.26X.
Amkor and AXT are both positioned to benefit from growing AI infrastructure spending, with AMKR benefiting from advanced packaging demand and AXTI from strong InP substrate demand for optical connectivity. AMKR's growth is supported by expanding AI/HPC packaging programs, strategic partnerships and capacity expansion across key manufacturing locations. AXTI, meanwhile, has a strong InP growth opportunity, supported by record revenues, a growing backlog and capacity expansion plans, but remains more exposed to external factors, including geopolitical and customer-related risks.
However, Amkor's stronger revenue scale, more diversified business, favorable valuation and solid earnings outlook make it a better pick for investors than AXTI, though both stocks sport a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) at present.

Amkor Technology Announces Phase 2 of Arizona Advanced Packaging and Test Campus; Expands Investment to $12 Billion
Strong customer commitments support 60,000 square meter expansion of U.S. advanced packaging capacity
TEMPE, Ariz.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sep. 8, 2026--
Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR), a leading provider of outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services, today announced phase 2 of its Arizona Advanced packaging and test campus. Driven by strong customer commitments that have surpassed the 33,000 square meters of cleanroom capacity planned for phase 1, the phase 2 expansion is expected to add 60,000 square meters and bring the campus to approximately 93,000 square meters of cleanroom space. The expansion increases the project’s planned investment to approximately $12 billion.
Designed from the outset as a multi-phase project, Amkor’s Arizona campus, which includes wafer bump, probe, assembly and test capabilities, is being developed to support long-term demand for advanced semiconductor packaging and test services in the U.S. Phase 2 expands manufacturing scale, and together with phase 1 is expected to support a workforce of more than 3,500 Arizona-based employees.
“This next phase reflects the confidence our customers have placed in Amkor, the critical role advanced packaging plays in enabling the future of semiconductor innovation, and the strategic importance of our Arizona campus,” said Kevin Engel, president and chief executive officer of Amkor Technology. “As chip architectures become more complex, customers need a trusted partner that can deliver at scale with the quality, technology leadership and operational discipline required for their most advanced products, and it is critical to have that capacity in the U.S.”
Amkor’s Arizona campus is the first OSAT production site in the U.S. for advanced packaging in high volume, giving customers access to a full domestic turnkey manufacturing platform. Construction of phase 2 is anticipated to begin late 2027, with completion expected by the end of 2029. Amkor’s Arizona 170-acre campus allows for further expansion as needed to support customer demand.

Amkor Technology Reports Financial Results for the Second Quarter 2026
TEMPE, Ariz. -- July 27, 2026 -- Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR), a leading provider of semiconductor packaging and test services, today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026.
•Net sales $1.90 billion, up 26% year-on-year
•Gross profit $319 million, operating income $200 million
•Net income $174 million, earnings per diluted share $0.70
“Amkor delivered record second quarter revenue and strong profitability, with record revenue in our Computing and Automotive & Industrial end markets," said Kevin Engel, president and chief executive officer. "During the first half of 2026, we expanded strategic partnerships across the semiconductor ecosystem, advanced key customer programs in AI and HPC, and continued the expansion of our Advanced packaging and test capacity. We expect these actions will strengthen our competitive position, increase our earnings power, and create sustainable shareholder value.”

Net income and earnings per diluted share also include a $16 million and $0.07 benefit, respectively.
At June 30, 2026, total cash and short-term investments was $2.5 billion, and total debt was $2.5 billion.
The company paid a quarterly dividend of $0.08352 per share on June 23, 2026. The declaration and payment of future dividends, as well as any record and payment dates, are subject to the approval of the Board of Directors.
The following information presents Amkor’s guidance for the third quarter 2026 (unless otherwise noted):
•Net sales of $1.95 billion to $2.05 billion

The live call can also be accessed by dialing 1-877-407-4019 or 1-201-689-8337.
About Amkor Technology, Inc.
Amkor Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMKR) is the world’s largest U.S. headquartered OSAT and is a global leader in outsourced semiconductor packaging and test services. With a strong track record of innovation, a broad and diverse geographic footprint and solid partnerships with lead customers, Amkor delivers high-quality solutions that enable the world’s leading semiconductor and electronics companies to bring advanced technologies to market. The company’s comprehensive portfolio includes advanced packaging, wafer-level processing, and system-in-package solutions targeting applications for smartphones, data centers, artificial intelligence, automobiles and wearables. For more information visit amkor.com.

Bitcoin mining stocks are surging at a rate that dwarfs the coin itself, and the gap between equity gains and spot price raises a question the tape alone cannot answer.
Published September 17, 2026, 9:34am ET · 4 min read

A golden Bitcoin coin stands prominently against a backdrop of financial candlestick charts and electrifying sparks, reflecting the cryptocurrency's journey following its past all-time high. © Morrowind / Shutterstock.com
TheBitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) mining complex is repricing faster than the coin itself Thursday morning, and CleanSpark sits near the front of that move. Those sector gains are running at multiples of Bitcoin’s own advance, which points to a sector-wide re-rating rather than a coin-driven bid.
The CoinShares Bitcoin Mining and Digital Power ETF (NASDAQ:WGMI) is up 6% to $47.20, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 1% to $763.81. Bitcoin is up 1.39% to $76,633.43 over the trailing 24 hours.
CleanSpark (NASDAQ:CLSK | CLSK Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $13.49 in Thursday morning trading, keeping CleanSpark near the front of a broader mining rally with no fresh company disclosure behind the move. Meanwhile, Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) shares are up 4% to $130.71, a smaller gain than the pure miners but still a multiple of the coin’s own advance.
The gap between the equity gains and Bitcoin’s own move is the story here. Bitcoin’s 1.39% advance doesn’t account for CleanSpark’s 5% jump, and the CoinShares fund’s matching 6% gain confirms that this is a group bid rather than a CleanSpark-specific reaction.
With no CleanSpark press release, filing or transcript landing this morning, the plain mechanism looks like a sector-wide re-rating of high-beta crypto equities. A short squeeze can’t be ruled out as a contributor, though no fresh short interest data verifies that read, and it stays a possible rather than a confirmed driver of CleanSpark’s tape.
CleanSpark’s 5% advance is running against a Bitcoin quote that has already given back ground from earlier month highs, so the equity bid isn’t simply a reflection of a strong coin session. That divergence is the pattern that keeps drawing attention to miner names when the group catches a bid, and CleanSpark’s move fits the profile.
The U.S. Senate cloture vote on the Clarity Act failed on September 15, when the measure fell short of the sixty votes it needed to advance. That defeat is two sessions old and crypto-linked equities rebounded the following session, which places it in the background of today’s move rather than the trigger for it.
Strategy, the corporate Bitcoin proxy in this group, tends to trade as leveraged exposure to the coin. Strategy’s 4% gain sitting below the pure miners’ moves is consistent with a bid concentrated in operating mining equities rather than treasury vehicles, and it reinforces the read that the sector, not the coin, is doing the work today.
CleanSpark’s bull case rests on the size of the gap between the equity moves and Bitcoin’s advance. A mining complex repricing faster than the coin suggests the market is paying for something beyond spot exposure, and CleanSpark’s version of that something is its data center build-out and the prospect of leasing capacity to artificial intelligence tenants.
The complication is that a move this size with no accompanying disclosure can unwind as fast as it arrived. CleanSpark’s gain matches the CoinShares fund almost exactly, which says the bid isn’t CleanSpark-specific and can reverse if the sector bid fades before the close.
The company’s operating profile leans on scaling its mining fleet while carving out space for adjacent digital infrastructure, and any signal that a large tenant sits behind the current data center footprint would change the story materially (we profiled seven suppliers riding the AI data-center buildout, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here). Absent such a signal today, CleanSpark’s move reads as market appetite for the theme rather than confirmation of the theme.
The bear case for CleanSpark is straightforward. Sector re-ratings without accompanying company news tend to fade, and CleanSpark’s high beta cuts both ways: a subsequent leg lower in Bitcoin, or simply an unwind of today’s sector bid, can pull CleanSpark stock back through $13 as quickly as it advanced above.
Investors can watch for whether CleanSpark stock holds at $13.40 through the afternoon. A hold at these levels keeps the technical picture constructive; a give-back into the red would confirm the morning move was a sector reflex rather than a durable re-rating for CleanSpark.
Traders may want to keep an eye on whether the CoinShares fund and CleanSpark stock stay coupled for the rest of the session, since a decoupling would flag a company-specific bid or seller worth investigating. Shareholders should size their positions to account for CLSK stock’s high beta and the risk that a single-day rally without company disclosure often mean-reverts inside a few sessions.

CleanSpark has completed the closing of $2.276 billion in senior secured notes.
The Bitcoin miner says proceeds will support data-center expansion and refinancing of existing credit facilities.
The financing has closed, making this different from an earlier announcement of a proposed debt raise.
CleanSpark has completed one of the largest financing transactions of the year for a publicly traded Bitcoin miner, closing $2.276 billion of senior secured notes.
The company announced the completed transaction late on September 25, moving the financing from a capital-markets proposal into cash that can now be deployed across the business.
CleanSpark Is Funding More Than Bitcoin Miners
CleanSpark says the proceeds will be used in part to expand its data-center infrastructure and refinance existing debt.
That distinction matters as the economics of the mining sector continue to change.
Bitcoin miners still earn revenue by operating ASIC hardware and selling or holding the BTC they produce.
But power contracts, substations, land and large data-center campuses have become valuable assets in their own right as demand for high-performance computing and AI infrastructure grows.
CleanSpark has been building around that overlap.
A large secured financing gives the company additional capital to expand sites without relying entirely on equity issuance or selling Bitcoin reserves.
The notes were placed with qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A, a structure commonly used by public companies to raise debt from large investors without conducting a conventional public bond offering.
Debt Gives Miners Capital, But It Also Changes The Risk
The size of the deal is notable.
Mining is a capital-intensive business, and borrowing more than $2 billion introduces a significant fixed obligation onto the balance sheet.
That can work well when operating cash flow is strong and infrastructure investment generates attractive returns.
It becomes more uncomfortable when Bitcoin prices fall, mining difficulty rises or power economics deteriorate.
That tension has always existed in the sector.
Mining companies need to spend heavily to stay competitive, but taking on too much capital-market risk can turn a downturn into a balance-sheet problem.
CleanSpark appears willing to make the trade.
The company has spent the past several years increasing scale, upgrading its fleet and accumulating infrastructure in the United States.
Closing the $2.276 billion financing gives it substantially more firepower to continue that strategy.
This is no longer a plan to raise money.
The transaction has been completed, and CleanSpark now has to show what that capital can produce.

CleanSpark Climbs 5% as Bitcoin Miners Outrun the Coin; Strategy Rises 4%
Bitcoin mining stocks are surging at a rate that dwarfs the coin itself, and the gap between equity gains and spot price raises a question the tape alone cannot answer.
Published September 17, 2026, 9:34am ET · 4 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A golden Bitcoin coin stands prominently against a backdrop of financial candlestick charts and electrifying sparks, reflecting the cryptocurrency's journey following its past all-time high. © Morrowind / Shutterstock.com
TheBitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) mining complex is repricing faster than the coin itself Thursday morning, and CleanSpark sits near the front of that move. Those sector gains are running at multiples of Bitcoin’s own advance, which points to a sector-wide re-rating rather than a coin-driven bid.
The CoinShares Bitcoin Mining and Digital Power ETF (NASDAQ:WGMI) is up 6% to $47.20, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 1% to $763.81. Bitcoin is up 1.39% to $76,633.43 over the trailing 24 hours.
CleanSpark (NASDAQ:CLSK | CLSK Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $13.49 in Thursday morning trading, keeping CleanSpark near the front of a broader mining rally with no fresh company disclosure behind the move. Meanwhile, Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) shares are up 4% to $130.71, a smaller gain than the pure miners but still a multiple of the coin’s own advance.
The gap between the equity gains and Bitcoin’s own move is the story here. Bitcoin’s 1.39% advance doesn’t account for CleanSpark’s 5% jump, and the CoinShares fund’s matching 6% gain confirms that this is a group bid rather than a CleanSpark-specific reaction.
With no CleanSpark press release, filing or transcript landing this morning, the plain mechanism looks like a sector-wide re-rating of high-beta crypto equities. A short squeeze can’t be ruled out as a contributor, though no fresh short interest data verifies that read, and it stays a possible rather than a confirmed driver of CleanSpark’s tape.
CleanSpark’s 5% advance is running against a Bitcoin quote that has already given back ground from earlier month highs, so the equity bid isn’t simply a reflection of a strong coin session. That divergence is the pattern that keeps drawing attention to miner names when the group catches a bid, and CleanSpark’s move fits the profile.
The U.S. Senate cloture vote on the Clarity Act failed on September 15, when the measure fell short of the sixty votes it needed to advance. That defeat is two sessions old and crypto-linked equities rebounded the following session, which places it in the background of today’s move rather than the trigger for it.
Strategy, the corporate Bitcoin proxy in this group, tends to trade as leveraged exposure to the coin. Strategy’s 4% gain sitting below the pure miners’ moves is consistent with a bid concentrated in operating mining equities rather than treasury vehicles, and it reinforces the read that the sector, not the coin, is doing the work today.
CleanSpark’s bull case rests on the size of the gap between the equity moves and Bitcoin’s advance. A mining complex repricing faster than the coin suggests the market is paying for something beyond spot exposure, and CleanSpark’s version of that something is its data center build-out and the prospect of leasing capacity to artificial intelligence tenants.
The complication is that a move this size with no accompanying disclosure can unwind as fast as it arrived. CleanSpark’s gain matches the CoinShares fund almost exactly, which says the bid isn’t CleanSpark-specific and can reverse if the sector bid fades before the close.
The company’s operating profile leans on scaling its mining fleet while carving out space for adjacent digital infrastructure, and any signal that a large tenant sits behind the current data center footprint would change the story materially (we profiled seven suppliers riding the AI data-center buildout, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here). Absent such a signal today, CleanSpark’s move reads as market appetite for the theme rather than confirmation of the theme.
The bear case for CleanSpark is straightforward. Sector re-ratings without accompanying company news tend to fade, and CleanSpark’s high beta cuts both ways: a subsequent leg lower in Bitcoin, or simply an unwind of today’s sector bid, can pull CleanSpark stock back through $13 as quickly as it advanced above.
Investors can watch for whether CleanSpark stock holds at $13.40 through the afternoon. A hold at these levels keeps the technical picture constructive; a give-back into the red would confirm the morning move was a sector reflex rather than a durable re-rating for CleanSpark.
Traders may want to keep an eye on whether the CoinShares fund and CleanSpark stock stay coupled for the rest of the session, since a decoupling would flag a company-specific bid or seller worth investigating. Shareholders should size their positions to account for CLSK stock’s high beta and the risk that a single-day rally without company disclosure often mean-reverts inside a few sessions.

CleanSpark Closes $2.276 Billion Senior Secured Notes Offering To Fund Sandersville Data Center Development
CleanSpark has completed its $2.276 billion senior secured notes offering, securing substantial debt financing to support the development of its data center in Sandersville, Georgia.
The notes were issued by CSDC Finance I, LLC, a wholly owned indirect subsidiary of CleanSpark, and carry an annual interest rate of 7.875%. The offering closed on September 25, 2026, with the notes scheduled to mature in October 2031.
The financing represents a major capital commitment to CleanSpark’s data center infrastructure business as the company develops large-scale computing facilities.
The notes were sold in a private offering to qualified institutional buyers and certain investors outside the United States.
They were issued at 98.5% of their $2.276 billion aggregate principal amount, meaning the cash received before expenses is lower than the notes’ face value.
CleanSpark intends to use the net proceeds to finance the remaining construction costs associated with its Sandersville data center, reimburse certain prior equity contributions related to the facility, and establish debt service reserves.
The financing was originally announced on September 18, when CleanSpark disclosed the pricing and expected closing date.
Completion of the offering establishes a dedicated source of long-term capital for the Sandersville project.
The financing has been structured at the subsidiary level, with CSDC Finance serving as the issuer.
The notes are fully and unconditionally guaranteed by CSRE Properties Sandersville, LLC, another CleanSpark subsidiary.
They are secured by first-priority liens on substantially all assets of the issuer and subsidiary guarantor, subject to specified exclusions.
The collateral package also includes the ownership interests in CSDC Finance held by its direct parent, CSDC Holdings I, LLC.
These arrangements establish the asset security supporting the debt and distinguish the offering from an unsecured corporate financing.
CleanSpark has also agreed to provide a completion guarantee for the Sandersville facility.
Under that arrangement, the parent company will provide additional funding if the bond proceeds and other available funds are insufficient to complete construction within the required timetable.
The guarantee provides an additional layer of support for the project during its development.
The notes will bear interest at 7.875% annually, with payments scheduled twice a year on April 1 and October 1.
The first interest payment is scheduled for April 1, 2027, and the notes will mature on October 1, 2031, unless redeemed or repurchased earlier under their terms.
The financing also includes provisions for scheduled principal amortization tied to the project’s debt service coverage requirements.
Following the project’s final commencement date, principal will be repaid semiannually in amounts designed to achieve the target project debt service coverage ratio specified in the bond documents.
The agreement contains customary covenants and events of default.
Certain changes in ownership may require the issuer to offer to repurchase the notes at 101% of their outstanding principal amount, plus accrued and unpaid interest.
The financing supports CleanSpark’s strategy of developing data center infrastructure capable of serving increasingly demanding computing applications.
CleanSpark reports controlling more than 1.8 gigawatts of power, land, and data center assets across the United States.
Its business combines experience in Bitcoin mining, energy infrastructure, and large-scale computing operations.
The company is pursuing opportunities to expand its data center platform as demand for computing capacity increases.
The Sandersville financing provides capital dedicated to completing a major facility within that infrastructure portfolio.
The transaction also establishes a financing structure under which the project’s assets and future cash flows support long-term debt obligations.
With the offering completed, CleanSpark will continue developing the Sandersville facility while managing the construction, financial, and operating commitments established under the notes.

CleanSpark has completed the closing of $2.276 billion in senior secured notes.
The Bitcoin miner says proceeds will support data-center expansion and refinancing of existing credit facilities.
The financing has closed, making this different from an earlier announcement of a proposed debt raise.
CleanSpark has completed one of the largest financing transactions of the year for a publicly traded Bitcoin miner, closing $2.276 billion of senior secured notes.
The company announced the completed transaction late on September 25, moving the financing from a capital-markets proposal into cash that can now be deployed across the business.
CleanSpark Is Funding More Than Bitcoin Miners
CleanSpark says the proceeds will be used in part to expand its data-center infrastructure and refinance existing debt.
That distinction matters as the economics of the mining sector continue to change.
Bitcoin miners still earn revenue by operating ASIC hardware and selling or holding the BTC they produce.
But power contracts, substations, land and large data-center campuses have become valuable assets in their own right as demand for high-performance computing and AI infrastructure grows.
CleanSpark has been building around that overlap.
A large secured financing gives the company additional capital to expand sites without relying entirely on equity issuance or selling Bitcoin reserves.
The notes were placed with qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A, a structure commonly used by public companies to raise debt from large investors without conducting a conventional public bond offering.
Debt Gives Miners Capital, But It Also Changes The Risk
The size of the deal is notable.
Mining is a capital-intensive business, and borrowing more than $2 billion introduces a significant fixed obligation onto the balance sheet.
That can work well when operating cash flow is strong and infrastructure investment generates attractive returns.
It becomes more uncomfortable when Bitcoin prices fall, mining difficulty rises or power economics deteriorate.
That tension has always existed in the sector.
Mining companies need to spend heavily to stay competitive, but taking on too much capital-market risk can turn a downturn into a balance-sheet problem.
CleanSpark appears willing to make the trade.
The company has spent the past several years increasing scale, upgrading its fleet and accumulating infrastructure in the United States.
Closing the $2.276 billion financing gives it substantially more firepower to continue that strategy.
This is no longer a plan to raise money.
The transaction has been completed, and CleanSpark now has to show what that capital can produce.

Should You Buy CleanSpark (CLSK) Stock Before Its AI Pivot Pays Off?
As digital infrastructure assets undergo a monumental shift and bitcoin miners are becoming AI landlords, CleanSpark Inc. (NASDAQ:CLSK) is attempting to pivot from a pure-play, volatile cryptocurrency miner into a contracted, high-performance compute host. While historical multi-year revenue growth and operational cash flow generation have remained tied to unpredictable crypto cycles, CleanSpark's evolving balance sheet health, long-term return on invested capital/ROIC, and free cash flow conversion profile now hinge on converting power-heavy infrastructure into predictable, long-duration lease streams.
Should You Buy CleanSpark (CLSK) Stock Before Its AI Pivot Pays Off?
That capital-intensive evolution reached a key milestone on September 18, when CleanSpark priced $2.276 billion in 7.875% senior secured notes due 2031 at 98.5% of face value to institutional buyers. This massive debt raise directly supports the company's fundamental transition: the proceeds are earmarked to complete construction at its Sandersville Facility, reimburse equity previously deployed into the site, and fund debt service reserves. Backed by first-priority liens on Sandersville assets and a CleanSpark completion guarantee, this financing provides the liquidity required to convert heavy capital expenditure into durable, recurring cash flows.
The strategic thesis behind Sandersville looks considerably more grounded than a standard mining facility expansion. On August 6, when CleanSpark released results for the quarter ended June 30, management disclosed a landmark 20-year, $6.6 billion triple-net lease at Sandersville with a high investment-grade tenant.
This contract secures two decades of contracted, non-mining revenue, insulating the facility from daily bitcoin price volatility. Furthermore, the equity portion for Sandersville is fully funded, and CleanSpark has already pre-paid and ordered long-lead equipment to ensure it hits its ready-for-service target date. Pre-ordering critical equipment hedges against supply chain delays that plague high-density data center buildouts, reinforcing management's drive to transform power capacity into stable, long-term cash flow compounding.
However, executing this infrastructure pivot carries substantial near-term balance sheet friction and margin pressure. For the fiscal quarter ended June 30, CleanSpark reported a challenging set of financial metrics: top-line revenue dropped 30.5% year-over-year to $138.0 million, down from $198.6 million in the prior-year period. Operating profitability and margins suffered heavily, swinging from net income of $257.4 million to a net loss of $239.8 million ($0.89 per basic share). Adjusted EBITDA experienced a sharp reversal, plunging to negative $113.0 million compared to positive $377.7 million a year earlier.
These margin compression pressures occurred before absorbing the new $2.276 billion debt issuance. As of June 30, CleanSpark already carried $1.8 billion in long-term debt against $2.7 billion in total assets. Adding nearly $2.3 billion in senior secured notes, issued at a discount with a near-8% interest coupon, significantly escalates the company's fixed annual debt service burden at a time when core bitcoin mining operations are generating negative GAAP earnings.
Institutional sentiment highlights a stark divide in market expectations. Hedge fund ownership increased from 37 funds to 42 funds in the most recent quarter, indicating that institutional investors are accumulating shares despite rising leverage. Conversely, short sellers have mounted a massive bet against the stock, pushing short interest to 42.81% of float.
Evaluating core investor questions, does CleanSpark's forward P/E multiple of 30.49x, as of September 24, make the stock cheap or expensive? A forward P/E above 30x is undeniably rich for a business currently generating negative GAAP net income and operating losses. The multiple assumes a rapid, flawless earnings recovery as Sandersville's $6.6 billion contracted revenue begins flowing through the income statement. The aggressive 42.81% short interest is driven by bears who believe the heavy debt service from the 7.875% coupon notes, combined with ongoing cash burn in bitcoin mining, will outpace the timeline required to bring Sandersville online.
CleanSpark is actively executing a high-stakes transition, converting crypto mining sites into institutional-grade infrastructure with contracted 20-year revenue streams. The $6.6 billion Sandersville lease and project completion guarantee represent tangible operational milestones toward that goal. However, funding this transition requires carrying $2.276 billion in expensive, heavily secured debt while the core mining segment faces cash-flow headwinds. For bullish investors, timely execution at Sandersville will unlock long-term cash flow compounding and validate the forward 30.49x earnings multiple. For bears, high interest obligations and mining losses present significant balance sheet risk if project timelines stall.
While we acknowledge the potential of CLSK as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.
In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR
In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.
The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.
It has been and continues to be the case that analysts employed by brokerage firms are overly optimistic with their recommendations. On the other hand, earnings estimate revisions are at the core of the Zacks Rank. And empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
In addition, the different Zacks Rank grades are applied proportionately to all stocks for which brokerage analysts provide current-year earnings estimates. In other words, this tool always maintains a balance among its five ranks.
There is also a key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank when it comes to freshness. When you look at the ABR, it may not be up-to-date. Nonetheless, since brokerage analysts constantly revise their earnings estimates to reflect changing business trends, and their actions get reflected in the Zacks Rank quickly enough, it is always timely in predicting future stock prices.
